newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Crash of U.S. cargo jet kills 24 in Ecuador.
newsitem.headline: Crash of U.S. cargo jet kills 24 in Ecuador.

text.p: Twenty-four people were killed and 60 injured when a U.S.-owned cargo jet burst into flames and crashed into a densely populated poor district of the Ecuadorean port of Manta, officials said on Wednesday.
The Boeing 707 crew -- three Americans and a Colombian -- died, but most of the victims were on the ground.

The Pacific city 290 miles (480 km) southeast of Quito was on the eve of a fiesta when the plane caught fire soon after takeoff and showered burning wreckage on the poor Dolorosa neighborhood at 11:40 p.m. EDT on Tuesday (0340 GMT on Wednesday).

The plane's wings and fuselage tore tin roofs off houses and smashed others to rubble in the crash. Rescue workers had to wait for daybreak before searching for bodies, because the plane ripped out electricity lines when it crashed.
"The death toll is still not definitive. It might rise as we sort through the rubble," Health Minister Marcelo Cruz told a news conference in the capital, Quito.
The minister said no further donations of medicines and supplies were necessary to cope with the victims, many of whom had severe burns.

Flaming wreckage rained on eight blocks of Dolorosa -- a tragically apt name meaning "painful" in Spanish. The parish church took the brunt of the crash and shielded some of the humble houses around it from even worse damage.

"The tragedy would have been much worse if the church had not taken the impact. It would have hit houses made of bricks and wood," one resident said. "One wing hit a building by the church, and as the wings are where the fuel is kept, it exploded in a sheet of flames."
"All of Manta was wrapped in flames because of the fuel," another witness, Miguel Narea Zea, told Reuters.
"Part of the wing ended up just near where we live," another said. "It dragged all the houses down until it smashed into a restaurant. The owner was there and was killed."
The city morgue housed a pile of charred corpses in body bags awaiting identification.
President Abdala Bucaram declared a day of mourning and flew to Manta to supervise the rescue operations.
"This is a very regrettable accident. Obviously Ecuadoran families have suffered the loss of their loved ones," he said.
Police patrolled Dolorosa to stop looting after 10 people were arrested for stealing from homes whose owners had fled.

The Boeing Co. said engine makers Pratt & Whitney and the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board would travel to Manta to help determine why the plane, delivered to American Airlines in 1967 and later converted to cargo use, went down.
Boeing spokesman Dick Schleh said the plane's 65,000 hours' flying time was "not particularly high."
The plane belonged to Millon Air, a Miami-based cargo carrier owned by a Colombian family. Million Air had no immediate comment on the crash.

The company operates cargo flights, mostly by charter, to Latin American destinations. In April 1995 a Millon Air DC-8 overran a runway in Guatemala City and crashed into a shantytown, killing at least six people on the ground.
